record.title: Beijing AI+ Conference reports launch of ReAct-Manip robot adaptation evaluation set
record.summary: An official Beijing AI+ Conference recap dated October 31 says the event launched ReAct-Manip, a robot operation-adaptation evaluation set. The recap names the benchmark but gives no technical specification, scores or model comparisons. A separate news report also describes the release. The PyPI ReAct-Manip v0.3 package has not been tied to the conference announcement, so its protocol and any capability implications remain unestablished.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: An official Beijing AI+ Conference recap dated October 31, 2026, says the event launched the Physical AI Operation Adaptation Evaluation Set (ReAct-Manip).

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The recap presents ReAct-Manip as a robot operation-adaptation evaluation benchmark; it supplies no task protocol, scores or model comparisons.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected sources do not bind the conference release to the ReAct-Manip v0.3 package, identify a versioned technical artifact, or establish benchmark validity, model performance, independent validation or real-world transfer.

evidence_gaps.description: The official event recap names ReAct-Manip but does not link a paper, code repository, dataset or versioned benchmark specification. The PyPI v0.3 package surfaced earlier has an unresolved project link and has not been tied to the conference announcement.
No protocol, task inventory, baselines, results, reliability analysis, independent validation or hardware transfer evidence was provided in the official recap or the news report inspected.

brief.importance_rationale: If it supplies a reproducible test of whether robot policies improve through feedback across sequential manipulation attempts, it could help evaluation teams distinguish adaptation from one-shot task completion. The present record establishes only a named benchmark launch; without a specification or results its consequence remains useful but narrow.
limitations: The source supports an official event launch account, not a technical evaluation of the benchmark.
The PyPI ReAct-Manip v0.3 package has not been linked to the conference release; its protocol details are not attributed to this event.
No scores, model comparisons, validation results, hardware tests or adoption outcomes were reported in the inspected sources.

technical.claimed_result: The organizer describes ReAct-Manip as an evaluation set for robot operation adaptation. No score or tested capability result is reported in the inspected sources.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official event recap documents that ReAct-Manip was named as one of the conference results launched on October 31, 2026.
technical.implementation_status: Conference launch reported. A versioned public artifact and its relationship to the PyPI ReAct-Manip package have not been confirmed.
technical.mechanism: The event recap gives no protocol detail. The intended adaptation mechanism and task design remain to be established from a technical specification.
technical.novelty: The launch is reported as a robot operation-adaptation evaluation set. Novelty relative to prior sequential manipulation and adaptation benchmarks is not established.
technical.regime: Robot manipulation evaluation as presented at the October 31, 2026 Beijing AI+ Conference; the exact simulator, hardware, tasks and policies are not specified in the event recap.
technical.reproducibility: Not established: no benchmark specification, data, code or versioned conference artifact was linked in the inspected sources.
technical.strongest_baseline: No baseline or comparison is reported in the official recap. The identity mismatch between the event-reported benchmark and PyPI ReAct-Manip v0.3 prevents importing that package's documentation as the event benchmark protocol.

brief.title: Beijing AI+ Conference reports launch of ReAct-Manip robot adaptation evaluation set
brief.why_it_matters: A reproducible test of learning from sequential manipulation feedback could help distinguish adaptive robot policies from systems that only succeed on a one-shot attempt. The current sources establish an announced benchmark, not a valid measure, improved robot capability or transfer to hardware.
